title: Phasors: A Rotating Arrow Becomes a Sinusoid
topic: Phasor representation of an AC voltage — a vector of length V_m rotating at angular frequency ω; its projection on the real axis traces v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ); two phasors at a fixed phase difference produce two sinusoids in lock-step

beats.narration: An AC voltage swings sinusoidally — but there's a clearer way to picture it: a rotating arrow.

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
How do you draw an AC voltage that's always changing?

beats.narration: Set up the complex plane. The voltage is an arrow of length V m, sitting at angle phi to the real axis.

elements.content: Re/Im axes centred
Reference circle radius V_m
Static phasor arrow at angle phi
V_m magnitude label along arrow
phi angle label between arrow and real axis
magnitude is the amplitude, angle is the phase

beats.narration: Now spin it. As the arrow rotates at omega, its projection on the real axis traces the cosine wave you see on the right.

elements.content: Complex plane on the left, sinusoid scope on the right
Phasor arrow rotating CCW at constant angular velocity
Projection drop-line from arrow tip down to the real axis
Sinusoid trace on the right plotting Re(arrow) vs time, drawn synchronously
Horizontal connector line from arrow projection to scope cursor
v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ) caption above scope

beats.narration: Add a second phasor lagging by ninety degrees. Both rotate together — and their two waves stay locked in phase difference.

elements.content: Two phasors at 90° apart, rotating together
Two sinusoid traces, one cosine one sine (90° lag)
V₁ and V₂ labels on each phasor
phase difference stays constant — algebra replaces calculus

beats.narration: Each AC voltage becomes one number — magnitude and angle — that you can add like a vector. No more integrating sines.

elements.content: magnitude · angle  →  add like vectors
the trick that makes AC analysis tractable
